about: Lessons and quizzes written from Script-2026 to close the gaps of notes/solid-state/coverage.md. Generated by notes/solid-state/build/gaps/build.py.

blocks.html: A crystal is a periodic arrangement that stretches across the whole sample: long-range order, although the interactions that produce it reach only nearest and next-nearest neighbours. A liquid has only local order that keeps fluctuating; a glass (amorphous solid) is local order that froze before the atoms found the periodic arrangement (script 1.1).

A unit cell is any volume that fills space without overlap when it is moved by all lattice translations $\mathbf R=n_1\mathbf a+n_2\mathbf b+n_3\mathbf c$. A primitive cell contains exactly one lattice point; a conventional cell is larger and shows the symmetry (the BCC cube holds 2 points, the FCC cube 4). The crystal is lattice plus basis: the group of atoms attached to every lattice point (script 1.2.1).

Symmetry operations leave the crystal unchanged and form a group. Besides translations there are point symmetries that keep one point fixed: inversion, mirror planes and rotations; a lattice allows only 1-, 2-, 3-, 4- and 6-fold axes. Combined with fractional translations this gives 17 symmetry groups in 2D and 230 in 3D (script 1.2.2).

Symmetry constrains every physical property. A crystal with an inversion centre cannot show circular dichroism (invert the whole universe: the crystal maps onto itself, the light reverses its handedness). In a cubic crystal the conductivity, thermal-conductivity and elastic tensors must have cubic symmetry, so the ellipsoid is a sphere: transport is isotropic. A tetragonal crystal may differ along and across its axis (script 1.2.2).

blocks.tex: \mathbf b_1=2\pi\frac{\mathbf a_2\times\mathbf a_3}{\mathbf a_1\cdot(\mathbf a_2\times\mathbf a_3)}\ \text{(cyclic)},\qquad \mathbf a_i\cdot\mathbf b_j=2\pi\delta_{ij},\qquad e^{i\mathbf G\cdot\mathbf R}=1
blocks.label: reciprocal lattice, script 1.3.1

blocks.html: Miller indices $(hkl)$ label a family of parallel lattice planes: one plane of the family cuts the axes at $\mathbf a/h$, $\mathbf b/k$, $\mathbf c/l$ (zero index: parallel to that axis). The reciprocal vector $\mathbf G_{hkl}=h\mathbf a^*+k\mathbf b^*+l\mathbf c^*$ is perpendicular to the planes, and neighbouring planes are $d_{hkl}=2\pi/|\mathbf G_{hkl}|$ apart (script 1.3.2; proof in sheet 8 Q1).
In a cubic lattice $[hkl]\perp(hkl)$, but not in general: the normal of a plane is always the reciprocal vector $\mathbf G_{hkl}$ (sheet 2 Q2).

check.q: What can the electrical conductivity tensor of a cubic crystal look like?
options: Zero except along the cube diagonals
check.explain: Cubic symmetry turns the ellipsoid of the tensor into a sphere: $\sigma_{ij}=\sigma\delta_{ij}$, isotropic conduction.

check.q: Which statement about a primitive unit cell is right?
options: It contains exactly one lattice point
It always shows the full symmetry of the lattice
check.explain: There are infinitely many primitive cells, all of the same volume; the Wigner–Seitz cell is one of them, and conventional cells are chosen when the symmetry matters.

check.q: The planes $(hkl)$ of a cubic crystal with $a=4$ Å: how far apart are the $(110)$ planes?

enc.title: Scattering vector, form factor and Friedel’s law

blocks.html: In a scattering experiment a wave with $\mathbf k_i$ leaves with $\mathbf k_f$; for elastic scattering $|\mathbf k_f|=|\mathbf k_i|$. What the sample decides is the amplitude as a function of the scattering vector $\mathbf q=\mathbf k_f-\mathbf k_i$: it is the Fourier transform of the scattering density at $\mathbf q$ (script 1.5.1–1.5.2).

blocks.tex: F(\mathbf q)=\sum_jf_j(\mathbf q)\,e^{i\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r_j},\qquad I\propto|F(\mathbf G)|^2\ \text{ only for }\ \mathbf q=\mathbf G
blocks.label: structure factor of the unit cell; Laue condition

blocks.html: X-rays scatter off the electron cloud, so each atom enters with its atomic form factor $f_j(\mathbf q)$, the Fourier transform of its electron density: it grows with the number of electrons and falls off at large $q$. Neutrons scatter off the nuclei, which are points on this scale: their scattering length does not depend on $q$, varies irregularly between elements and isotopes (light atoms visible), and neutrons also see magnetic moments (script 1.5.4).

Friedel’s law: the scattering density is real, $\rho(\mathbf r)=\rho^*(\mathbf r)$, so $F(-h,-k,-l)=F^*(h,k,l)$ and $I(h,k,l)=I(-h,-k,-l)$. It holds even when the crystal has no inversion centre: diffraction alone cannot tell a crystal from its inverted copy (script eq. 1.35).

Every symmetry of $\rho$ shows in the intensities: a mirror $\rho(x,y,z)=\rho(x,y,-z)$ gives $I(h,k,l)=I(h,k,-l)$; a 4-fold axis gives $I(k,-h,l)=I(h,k,l)$. A non-primitive cell gives systematic absences: BCC, $F=0$ for $h+k+l$ odd; FCC, $F=0$ unless $h,k,l$ are all even or all odd (script 1.5.3).
Typical exam step: write $F$ for the given basis, find the absent reflections, then use $I\propto|F|^2$ to compare intensities.

check.q: A crystal without an inversion centre. Are $I(h,k,l)$ and $I(-h,-k,-l)$ equal?
options: Yes: Friedel’s law only needs a real scattering density
No: only centrosymmetric crystals give equal intensities
check.explain: $F(-\mathbf G)=F^*(\mathbf G)$ because $\rho$ is real, so $|F|^2$ is the same.

check.q: Which reflection is absent for an FCC lattice with one atom per lattice point?
check.explain: FCC needs $h,k,l$ unmixed (all even or all odd); $(110)$ is mixed.

questions.q: How many crystallographic symmetry groups exist in three dimensions?
questions.explain: 230 space groups (17 in 2D). 14 is the number of Bravais lattices, 32 the number of point groups.

questions.q: Why do neutrons see hydrogen in a crystal much better than X-rays?
options: They scatter off nuclei with a scattering length that does not grow with the number of electrons
They carry no charge, so they reach deeper
questions.explain: X-ray form factors grow with the electron count, so hydrogen (one electron) is nearly invisible; nuclear scattering lengths are of similar size for all elements.

questions.q: A mirror plane $z\to-z$ in the crystal implies for the Bragg intensities:
questions.explain: Symmetries of $\rho$ carry over to $|F|^2$ (script 1.5.3).

questions.q: A glass differs from a crystal by
questions.explain: Locally a glass looks much like a liquid, frozen; it has no periodic order across the sample (script 1.1).

blocks.html: Covalent bond, starting from H$_2^+$ (two protons, one electron): combine the atomic orbitals $\phi_A$, $\phi_B$ (LCAO). The symmetric combination piles charge up between the protons and lowers the energy (bonding); the antisymmetric one has a node between them and raises it (antibonding). In H$_2$ both electrons, with opposite spins, sit in the bonding orbital (script 1.6.4; sheet 3 Q3 does this with delta wells).

blocks.label: bonding (+) and antibonding (−); splitting 2t set by the overlap

blocks.html: Covalent bonds are directional: they point where the orbitals overlap. Carbon and silicon mix s and p orbitals into four sp$^3$ hybrids at tetrahedral angles (diamond, Si, Ge); graphene uses three sp$^2$ hybrids in a plane. Directional bonds give open structures with few neighbours (diamond: 4).

Hydrogen bond: hydrogen covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom (O, N) loses most of its electron and sticks out as a nearly bare proton, which attracts an electronegative atom of a neighbouring molecule. The proton is so small that it can couple only two atoms. It holds ice and DNA strands together and folds proteins (script 1.6.5).

Metallic bond: the outer orbitals of all atoms merge into orbitals spanning the sample; their electrons move freely (one or two per atom, measured by the Hall effect), the inner ones stay on the ions. The binding comes mainly from the lower kinetic energy of delocalised electrons. It is not directional, so metals pack densely: FCC, HCP, or BCC (filling 0.68) (script 1.6.6).
Order of cohesive energies per atom (week-3 lecture question): van der Waals (Ar ≈ 0.08 eV) < metallic (Na ≈ 1.1 eV) < ionic (NaCl ≈ 3.3 eV) < covalent (diamond ≈ 7.4 eV).

check.q: Why does a hydrogen bond link only two atoms?
options: The bare proton is so small that only two ions fit next to it
Hydrogen has only one electron to share
check.explain: Script 1.6.5: a proton has no electrons, so it is much smaller than any ion and cannot have more than two nearest neighbours.

check.q: Why do elemental metals crystallise in close-packed structures?
options: The metallic bond has no preferred direction
The electrons are localised on the atoms
Covalent bonds between neighbours are strongest in FCC
Close packing minimises the Fermi energy
check.explain: Like the non-directional van der Waals bond of noble gases, the metallic bond rewards having as many neighbours as possible.

options: has a node between the protons and a higher energy
has more charge between the protons
is occupied by both electrons in H$_2$

enc.title: Phonon momentum, decay and how phonons are measured

blocks.html: A phonon of wave vector $\mathbf q$ carries quasi-momentum $\hbar\mathbf q$: it is defined only up to a reciprocal lattice vector, because $\mathbf q$ and $\mathbf q+\mathbf G$ describe the same displacements. In inelastic scattering, energy and quasi-momentum are conserved: for a phonon created, $\hbar\omega_i-\hbar\omega_f=\hbar\omega(\mathbf q)$ and $\mathbf k_i-\mathbf k_f=\mathbf q+\mathbf G$. Processes that need $\mathbf G\neq0$ to bring $\mathbf q$ back into the first Brillouin zone are called Umklapp processes (script 2.3.2).

Anharmonic lattice (script 2.3.3): with terms beyond second order in the potential, a normal mode slowly passes its energy to other modes. It decays like a damped oscillator, $e^{i(\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r-\omega t)}\to e^{i(\mathbf q\cdot\mathbf r-\omega t)}e^{-\gamma t}$. In terms of phonons: a phonon falls apart, most often into two, conserving energy and quasi-momentum. No energy is lost: all forces are conservative, it only moves between modes. Anharmonicity also causes thermal expansion and keeps the thermal conductivity finite.

Measuring phonons (script 2.3.4): a monochromator crystal Bragg-reflects only one wave number out of a white beam, $\sin\theta_m=|\mathbf K_m|/(2k_i)$ (eq. 2.59). After the sample, an analyzer crystal passes only one $k_f$ to the detector: the three-axis spectrometer, full control of $\mathbf k_i$ and $\mathbf k_f$ but one final energy at a time. For neutrons there is also time of flight: a pulsed beam, and $k_f$ of every neutron follows from its detector position and arrival time; no neutrons are wasted.

Why neutrons and not X-rays for phonons: a thermal neutron with a wavelength of a few Å has an energy of a few meV, comparable to phonon energies, so a phonon changes its energy by a measurable fraction. An X-ray photon of the same wavelength has keV.

check.q: An inelastic peak gets broader on heating. What does the width measure?
options: The inverse lifetime of the phonon (anharmonic decay)
check.explain: A decaying mode gives a Lorentzian line whose half-width is the decay rate $\gamma$ (script 2.3.3).

check.q: What does the analyzer of a three-axis spectrometer select?
options: The final wave number $k_f$ that reaches the detector

enc.title: Script check: phonon momentum and anharmonicity

questions.q: An Umklapp process is one in which
options: quasi-momentum is conserved only up to a reciprocal lattice vector $\mathbf G\neq0$
a phonon is created and destroyed at once
the phonon leaves the first Brillouin zone for good
questions.explain: $\mathbf k_i-\mathbf k_f=\mathbf q+\mathbf G$ with $\mathbf G\ne0$: the result is folded back into the first zone.

questions.q: In a perfectly harmonic crystal, phonons
options: never decay and do not interact
have a finite lifetime set by temperature
questions.explain: Normal modes are exact eigenstates of the harmonic Hamiltonian; decay needs anharmonic terms.

questions.q: Which of these is a consequence of anharmonicity?
options: The $T^3$ law of the specific heat
questions.explain: In a harmonic potential the average atomic position does not change with amplitude; the asymmetric (anharmonic) potential makes the lattice expand.

questions.q: When a phonon decays into two, what is conserved?
questions.explain: Script 2.3.3: energy only moves between modes; the decay products carry the original energy and quasi-momentum.

enc.title: Chemical potential, interactions, quasiparticles and ARPES

blocks.html: The chemical potential $\mu$ fixes the number of electrons at a given temperature. In a metal $k_BT\ll\epsilon_F$ (Fermi temperatures of $10^4$–$10^5$ K), so $\mu$ stays practically at $\epsilon_F$; only states within a few $k_BT$ of $\epsilon_F$ are partly occupied.

Why interactions can be ignored (script 3.1.5): two electrons near $\epsilon_F$ can only scatter into empty states, and those lie within about $k_BT$ of the Fermi surface. The number of allowed pairs of final states goes like $[\nu(\epsilon_F)k_BT]^2$, so the electron–electron scattering rate is $\propto T^2$ and vanishes at low temperature: Pauli blocking makes the electron gas nearly ideal.

Tight binding (script 3.2.3): electrons hop between atomic orbitals with the hopping (overlap) amplitude $t$. In 1D, $E(k)=E_0-2t\cos ka$: a band of width $4t$. More overlap, wider band; next-nearest neighbours add $-2t^\prime\cos2ka$ (sheet 7 Q3).

Quasiparticles (script 3.3): phonons are excitations (the ground state has none); electrons are real particles (the ground state has all of them). The elementary excitations of a metal are quasielectrons, an extra electron at $\mathbf k$ outside the Fermi sea, and quasiholes, a missing electron inside it. Their energy is fixed by their momentum, unlike a particle–hole pair, which can have the same momentum at very different energies.

blocks.label: script eq. (3.68); quasiholes are defined inside the Fermi sea with positive energy too

blocks.html: ARPES (script 3.4): an X-ray photon is absorbed and an electron leaves the sample. From the measured $\mathbf p_f$ and $E_f=p_f^2/2m_e$: momentum transfer $\Delta\mathbf p=\hbar\mathbf k_i-\mathbf p_f$ and energy transfer $\Delta E=\hbar\omega_i-p_f^2/2m_e$, carried by the quasihole left behind. Intensity peaks at $\Delta E=\tilde\varepsilon(\Delta\mathbf p/\hbar)$: the dispersion. At zero energy transfer only momenta on the Fermi surface give a signal: ARPES maps Fermi surfaces. It probes only the surface, needs ultra-high vacuum, freshly cleaved crystals and a synchrotron.

check.q: Why is the electron–electron scattering rate in a metal $\propto T^2$?
options: Both scattered electrons must end in empty states within about $k_BT$ of the Fermi surface
The Coulomb force falls off as $1/r^2$
The number of phonons grows as $T^2$
check.explain: Script 3.1.5: the phase space of allowed final states is $\propto(k_BT)^2$.

options: Quasiholes: their dispersion and the Fermi surface
Quasielectrons far above the Fermi energy
check.explain: Only occupied states can emit an electron, so ARPES sees the states below $\epsilon_F$ (quasiholes), plus a thin layer above at finite $T$.

enc.title: Script check: Fermi gas, quasiparticles, ARPES

questions.q: Why is a particle–hole pair not a quasiparticle?
options: Pairs with the same momentum can have very different energies
questions.explain: A quasiparticle needs a unique energy for each momentum (a dispersion); particle–hole pairs form a continuum (script 3.3, Fig. 3.7).

questions.q: In a 1D tight-binding band $E=E_0-2t\cos ka$, what is the band width?
questions.explain: From $E_0-2t$ at $k=0$ to $E_0+2t$ at $k=\pi/a$.

questions.q: ARPES has to be done in ultra-high vacuum because
options: it probes only the surface, which must stay clean
the X-rays are absorbed by air
questions.explain: The ejected electrons come from the top atomic layers; any oxide or adsorbate changes what is measured (script 3.4).

questions.q: How does the chemical potential of a metal change between 0 and 300 K?
questions.explain: At room temperature $k_BT\approx25$ meV against $\epsilon_F$ of several eV.

enc.title: Band electrons carry current and heat; screening

blocks.html: Conductivity of band electrons (script 4.2.4): a field $\mathbf E$ shifts the whole Fermi sea by $-e\mathbf E\tau/\hbar$ in $k$ space before scattering resets it. The net current comes from the extra right-movers and missing left-movers, all near the Fermi surface.

The result looks like Drude, but for a different reason: in Drude all electrons drift slowly; in the band picture only a fraction $\sim k_BT/\epsilon_F$ contributes, each moving at $v_F$, faster by the inverse factor. The factor $n_e$ is a coincidence of the free-electron counting.

Thermal conductivity (script 4.3): in a temperature gradient the right-movers near $\epsilon_F$ come from the colder side and the left-movers from the hotter side; scattering limits the imbalance after a time $\tau$. The same electrons carry heat and charge, so the ratio is universal: the Wiedemann–Franz law.

Screening (script 4.4): an extra charge $Q$ in a metal pulls in a cloud of conduction electrons of total charge $-Q$. A slowly varying potential $\phi$ shifts the bands by $-e\phi$ at a fixed Fermi energy, so the local density changes by $\delta n=e\phi\,\nu(\epsilon_F)$; with Poisson’s equation this gives the screened (Yukawa) potential.

For copper ($n_e=8.5\cdot10^{22}$ cm$^{-3}$) $r_0\approx0.55$ Å: charges in neighbouring cells barely feel each other. With few states at the Fermi energy (nearly empty or nearly full band) the screening length grows to many lattice spacings.

Script eq. (4.46) also gives a free-electron form of $r_0^2$; in the PDF it reads $\frac14(n_e/a_0)^{-1/3}$, which does not have the units of an area. Use $r_0^2=\varepsilon_0/(e^2\nu(\epsilon_F))$ with $\nu(\epsilon_F)=\frac{3n_e}{2\epsilon_F}$, equivalently $r_0^2=\frac{\pi a_0}{4k_F}$; both give the 0.55 Å for copper.

check.q: In the band picture, which electrons carry the electric current?
options: Only those near the Fermi surface
All conduction electrons, each drifting slowly
Only the electrons at the bottom of the band
check.explain: Script 4.2.4: the shifted Fermi sea differs from the equilibrium one only near the Fermi surface.

check.q: What is the Lorenz number $\kappa/(\sigma T)$ of a metal?
options: It depends on the scattering time

check.q: The Thomas–Fermi screening length gets longer when
options: the density of states at $\epsilon_F$ gets smaller

enc.title: Script check: band transport, heat and screening

questions.q: In an electric field, in the steady state, the Fermi sea is
questions.explain: Acceleration $\hbar\dot{\mathbf k}=-e\mathbf E$ for a time $\tau$, then scattering (script Fig. 4.6).

questions.q: A metal’s thermal conductivity doubles when cooled. If Wiedemann–Franz holds, its electrical conductivity
options: more than doubles, since $\sigma=\kappa/(LT)$ and $T$ also fell
questions.explain: $\sigma=\kappa/(LT)$: with $\kappa\times2$ and $T$ smaller, $\sigma$ grows by more than 2.

questions.q: The screened potential of a point charge in a metal falls off
questions.explain: Yukawa form, script eq. (4.45).

questions.q: Why does the Drude formula give the right conductivity although its picture is wrong?
options: Fewer electrons (those near $\epsilon_F$) move faster ($v_F$): the two factors cancel
questions.explain: Script 4.2.4: a fraction $\sim k_BT/\epsilon_F$ of the electrons, moving at $v_F\gg v_{\text{thermal}}$.

blocks.html: Solar cell (script 5.4.5): light with $\hbar\omega>\Delta$ creates an electron–hole pair. In the depletion layer the built-in field sweeps the electron to the n side and the hole to the p side. The separated charge builds up a voltage, and through an external resistor the junction drives a current as long as it is lit. For Si: wavelengths below about $1.2\ \mu$m.

LED: the reverse process. A forward bias lowers the barrier, electrons flood into the p side and holes into the n side, and they recombine. Each recombination releases $\Delta$, as heat or as one photon with $\hbar\omega\approx\Delta$: nearly monochromatic light.

Momentum decides which materials glow. A photon of visible or infrared light has a wave vector tiny compared with the Brillouin zone, so a one-photon recombination needs the conduction minimum and the valence maximum at the same $\mathbf k$: a direct gap (GaAs, about 800 nm, infrared LEDs; GaP, 550 nm, green). Silicon has an indirect gap: it absorbs light well enough for solar cells but makes a poor LED. White LEDs are often UV LEDs on a phosphor.

check.q: Why is silicon a poor material for LEDs?
options: Its gap is indirect: recombination needs a phonon to supply momentum
check.explain: Script 5.4.5: the photon carries almost no momentum, so only direct-gap materials emit efficiently.

enc.title: Ferromagnetism of metals (Stoner) and Hund’s rules

blocks.html: Why metals like iron are ferromagnetic (script 6.2.5): the magnetic dipole interaction between electrons is about 0.1 meV (≈ 1 K), far too weak for a Curie temperature of 1043 K. The cause is the Coulomb repulsion combined with the Pauli principle: electrons with equal spins avoid each other anyway, electrons with opposite spins can come close and repel strongly. Effectively there is a short-range repulsion only between opposite spins in the same unit cell (Hubbard model).

In the mean-field approximation each spin species feels the average occupation of the other: a magnetisation acts like an extra internal field and enhances the Pauli susceptibility. When the enhancement diverges, the metal magnetises spontaneously: the Stoner instability.

Both $U$ and $\nu(\epsilon_F)$ are properties of the material: a large density of states at the Fermi energy (narrow d bands of Fe, Co, Ni) favours ferromagnetism; Cu and Ag have broad s bands and stay paramagnetic. At high temperature the criterion fails and the material turns paramagnetic at $T_C$.

Insulators (script 6.3): the magnetic electrons stay on their ions, and the size of each ion’s spin is set by Hund’s rules, standard atomic physics that the script refers to: (1) maximise the total spin $S$; (2) then maximise $L$; (3) $J=|L-S|$ for a shell less than half full, $J=L+S$ for more than half full. Only the spin direction remains free: a lattice of spins coupled by exchange.

check.q: Why can the magnetic dipole interaction not explain the ferromagnetism of iron?
options: It is about 0.1 meV, i.e. about 1 K, but iron stays magnetic up to 1043 K
It is screened by the conduction electrons
check.explain: Script 6.2.5: the energy scale is three orders of magnitude too small; the real cause is Coulomb repulsion plus Pauli.

check.q: According to the Stoner criterion, a metal becomes ferromagnetic when
check.explain: Script eq. (6.32): strong on-site repulsion and many states at the Fermi energy.

questions.q: In the Hubbard term $U\sum_jn_{j,+}n_{j,-}$, which electrons repel?
options: Two electrons of opposite spin in the same unit cell
questions.explain: Equal spins are kept apart by Pauli already; the effective extra repulsion acts on opposite spins in the same cell.

questions.q: Interactions change the Pauli susceptibility of a metal how?
options: They enhance it, and it diverges at the Stoner instability
questions.explain: Script eq. (6.30): denominator $1-\dots\chi_P$ with $U>0$.

questions.q: Fe$^{3+}$ has five 3d electrons. What is its spin by Hund’s first rule?
questions.explain: Five orbitals, one electron each with parallel spins: $S=5\cdot\frac12$.

questions.q: Why are Fe, Co and Ni ferromagnetic but Cu is not?
options: Narrow d bands give a large density of states at the Fermi energy
Cu has a larger Hubbard U
questions.explain: The Stoner criterion needs $UV_0\nu(\epsilon_F)>2$; Cu has a broad s band at $\epsilon_F$.
